images.alt: A long narrow dug-out canoe on a beach, with pairs of booms through the gunwale running out to a float
images.caption: A Bloomfield River dug-out on the beach: the double booms pass straight through the gunwale and run down to the crossed pegs in the float. Roth's photograph, the only old picture of a Kuku Yalanji canoe on this page.
images.credit: Photograph: W. E. Roth, North Queensland Ethnography Bulletin 14 (Records of the Australian Museum 8, 1910), Plate VI fig. 2

images.alt: Line drawing of two crossed pegs set into a float with the two halves of a double boom lashed above and below the crossing
images.caption: How the boom meets the float at Cape Bedford: two pegs morticed into the float and crossed, with the two halves of the double boom lashed above and below the angle. The Bloomfield canoe was built the same way.
images.credit: Drawing: W. E. Roth, North Queensland Ethnography Bulletin 14 (Records of the Australian Museum 8, 1910), fig. 13

images.alt: Line drawing of a dug-out seen from the outrigger side with seven pairs of booms pegged through a side board down to the float
images.caption: The Flinders-to-Endeavour type from the outrigger side: wash-boards lashed along the gunwale, with seven double booms pegged through them to the float. Bloomfield canoes had the booms but not the boards.
images.credit: Drawing: W. E. Roth, North Queensland Ethnography Bulletin 14 (Records of the Australian Museum 8, 1910), fig. 12

images.alt: Line drawing of a dug-out with two booms and a float on each side and a lattice staging between the booms
images.caption: The original double-outrigger dug-out of the Batavia (Wenlock) River, far to the north: two booms, a float each side and a central staging. Southward one float was dropped and the booms multiplied.
images.credit: Drawing: W. E. Roth, North Queensland Ethnography Bulletin 14 (Records of the Australian Museum 8, 1910), fig. 10

images.alt: Line drawing of a folded sheet of bark with one end clamped upright between two tied switches
images.caption: The Tully River bark canoe in its 'vice': the folded bark sheet clamped between two switches driven into the ground while the bow is cut and sewn. A neighbouring method; no bark canoe is recorded on Kuku Yalanji country.
images.credit: Drawing: W. E. Roth, North Queensland Ethnography Bulletin 14 (Records of the Australian Museum 8, 1910), fig. 4

images.alt: Line drawing of a lens-shaped bark canoe with sewn seams and a stick across the middle
images.caption: A three-sheet bark canoe of the Whitsunday Islands: one sheet for the bottom, two for the sides, sewn along the seams and held open with a cross-stick.
images.credit: Drawing: W. E. Roth, North Queensland Ethnography Bulletin 14 (Records of the Australian Museum 8, 1910), fig. 9
